acceptable.choice: Pay for a hosted volunteer-scheduling service (e.g. Better Impact, Rosterfy, Bloomerang Volunteer, Galaxy Digital, VolunteerHub, SignUpGenius Pro, Rota-style shift tools), with the contractor's month spent on choosing, setting up, importing data, training staff and writing a handover guide
acceptable.why: Shift sign-up, seeing gaps and reminders are a solved problem; the vendor handles hosting, security and updates, staff manage it through web admin pages, and any future contractor or even a volunteer can look after it without reading code.

acceptable.choice: Use a mainstream no-code database such as Airtable, or Microsoft Lists/Forms/Power Automate under a non-profit Microsoft 365 grant, set up with forms, views and automated reminders
acceptable.why: This is a fallback if no ready-made product fits: it is cheap, many contractors know it, and staff can edit it, but access control, plan limits and fragile automations must be checked and written down.

acceptable.choice: Install a well-known, actively maintained WordPress scheduling or volunteer plugin on WordPress hosting that is fully updated and managed
acceptable.why: WordPress contractors are cheap and easy to find and staff already know the admin pages, but this only works if the old site is brought up to date, kept patched automatically and properly secured first.

acceptable.choice: Only if no product fits: a small custom app in a very common, boring stack (Laravel/PHP or Django) on a managed platform (managed hosting or a PaaS with managed database and backups), using a standard SMS/email provider
acceptable.why: A common stack on managed hosting is the custom option a cheap future contractor is most likely to be able to take over, but it still has to be patched, paid for and looked after forever, so it should be the last resort.

ruled_out.choice: A bespoke system in the contractor's preferred modern stack (e.g. React/Next.js SPA + Node API, microservices, serverless functions spread across AWS)
ruled_out.why: Nobody on staff can look after it and the next low-budget contractor may not know that stack, so it breaks 'next contractor can pick it up' and 'works with little care'.

ruled_out.choice: A self-managed VPS or server (DigitalOcean droplet, EC2, Kubernetes, Docker you run yourself)
ruled_out.why: Someone has to patch the OS, renew certificates and run backups, and nobody will, which puts volunteers' personal data at risk.
Costly to build and keep in app stores, and too much for a month's work; a mobile-friendly website or the vendor's app does the job.

ruled_out.choice: Bolting custom code or old/abandoned plugins onto the existing years-old WordPress site as it is
ruled_out.why: Putting names and phone numbers on an unpatched, unmaintained site is a data-protection and security risk.

ruled_out.choice: A shared Google Sheet / Excel file opened by link, or WhatsApp groups as the system of record
ruled_out.why: Anyone with the link can see personal data, there is no role-based access or audit trail, phone numbers are shown to everyone, and it falls apart with 150 volunteers across several sites.

ruled_out.choice: Proprietary app builders that need specialist skills (e.g. Bubble, heavy Google Apps Script or custom Power Apps code)
ruled_out.why: The next generalist contractor may not be able to maintain it, and it can lock the charity in to one platform or break silently when quotas or pricing change.

ruled_out.choice: Accounts, domain, hosting or code repository held in the contractor's name
ruled_out.why: When the contractor leaves, the charity loses control of its system and data.

must_mention: Recommend buying and setting up an existing volunteer-scheduling product before building custom software, and say plainly that building is a last resort for this team.
Compare total cost of ownership: a subscription (many have non-profit discounts) against the hidden yearly cost of hosting, patching and paying a contractor to fix custom code.

The organisation must own every account and credential (vendor admin, domain, email/SMS provider, any hosting or repo), use its own email addresses for them, turn on MFA, and have at least two staff admins.

Data protection: collect only the data you need, give access by role (coordinators see only their food bank), sign a data processing agreement with the vendor, check where the data is hosted (e.g. UK/EU if UK GDPR applies), state a lawful basis or consent and a privacy notice, set retention and deletion rules, and have a way to remove people who leave.
The contract should require a plain-English handover: a runbook for staff, an admin guide, a list of where everything lives and how much it costs, and how to export the data.
Data must be exportable (CSV) and there must be a way out if the vendor raises prices or shuts down.
SMS reminders cost money per message and need opt-in; email reminders may be enough for some volunteers, so ask about this.
Volunteers should be able to sign up from a phone without installing anything; check accessibility and ease of use with real coordinators before committing.
Spend the contractor's month mostly on choosing the product, configuring it, importing data, training staff and documenting, not on writing code.
red_flags: Recommending a custom-built app in a trendy or niche stack, or letting the contractor choose whatever they like, without weighing who will maintain it.
Suggesting self-hosting, a VPS or containers for a team with nobody technical.
Storing volunteers' personal data on the old, unpatched WordPress site.
Ignoring data protection, or claiming that using a big vendor makes them automatically compliant.
Leaving accounts, code or hosting under the contractor's control, or not mentioning handover and documentation.
Recommending an open shared spreadsheet or group chat as the system that holds the personal data.
Ignoring running costs (subscription, SMS charges, hosting) or the charity's limited budget.
Recommending native mobile apps or a heavy architecture far beyond what 150 volunteers need.
Giving a confident single product pick without asking the charity to check that it fits their workflow, budget and data-location needs.
unknowns: Ongoing budget: whether they can afford a monthly subscription (and SMS charges) or only a one-off payment.
Which country's law applies (e.g. UK GDPR) and whether data must be hosted in a particular region.
Whether reminders must be SMS or email is acceptable, and whether every volunteer has a smartphone or email address.
How complex the shifts are: number of food banks and coordinators, recurring shifts, skills or roles, minimum staffing, swaps and cancellations.
Whether they already have Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 non-profit grants that could be used.
The state of the current WordPress site and its hosting, and who controls it now.
Whether volunteers will accept creating an account, or need a no-login sign-up.
Whether the system must connect to other tools (donor CRM, the website, mailing list), and whether accessibility or language support is needed.
Whether an off-the-shelf product actually fits their workflow, which can only be found out by trialling two or three with coordinators.
